disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation, is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, impulsivity, and difficulty inhibiting behavior, with comparatively fewer or less prominent inattentive features. In adults, the presentation often shifts from overt running and climbing to inner restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, and acting without forethought in work and social contexts. Symptoms must be present for at least six months, cause clinically significant impairment in multiple settings, and are typically rooted in childhood, even if they become more impairing or noticeable in adulthood due to increased role demands. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by its early onset, pervasive pattern of disinhibition and activity level, and the absence of episodic mood changes as the primary driver of difficulties.

narrative.personality: Willard is an outgoing, highly organized engineer who enjoys leading teams and packing his schedule with social sports and intellectually stimulating hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Willard was promoted from a primarily analytical role into a lead position on a high-visibility launch vehicle program, which shifted his workday from long, solitary modeling sessions to back-to-back design reviews, stakeholder meetings, and safety briefings. The new role demanded prolonged periods of sitting through formal presentations and maintaining focus on detailed discussions, while he also tried to keep up his packed after-work schedule of sports, meetups, and late-night problem-solving sessions. Over the following year, he found it increasingly difficult to stay in conference rooms and remain engaged during lengthy technical and budget meetings, which began to frustrate colleagues and draw criticism from his manager about his professionalism and reliability in leadership settings. As his performance reviews started to mention concerns about his behavior in formal settings and his own anxiety about jeopardizing the promotion grew, he agreed to seek psychiatric evaluation at the suggestion of a trusted coworker who noticed how much he struggled with staying put in structured work situations.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to stay in my seat during long meetings anymore, even when I know I’m supposed to.”

narrative.personality: Timothy is a patient, detail-oriented retiree who takes pride in careful record-keeping, hands-on projects, and steady involvement in his church and community.
narrative.stressor: Roughly a year and a few months ago, Timothy fully retired from part-time farm consulting and shifted into a slower-paced routine centered on church treasury work, genealogy, and tending a small garden instead of managing a busy farm. The abrupt reduction in physically demanding tasks and structured outdoor labor left him spending long stretches of time seated at a desk balancing accounts, attending choir practices, and sitting through lengthy church committee meetings. In this quieter phase of life, he became acutely aware of how uncomfortable and agitated he felt when trying to sit still for these obligations, often needing to get up, pace, or find small tasks to keep his body occupied, which began to disrupt meetings and worry his fellow congregants. When his wife commented that his constant need to move and inability to sit through services was wearing on both of them and might be more than just “nervous energy,” he agreed to see a psychiatrist to understand why he felt so keyed up despite being ostensibly retired and at ease.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Even in church or meetings, I feel so restless I can’t just sit there anymore.”

narrative.personality: Edileusa is an energetic, conscientious supervisor who thrives on social interaction, dancing, and self-improvement while juggling work responsibilities with an active nightlife.
narrative.stressor: Around fourteen months ago, Edileusa was promoted from caregiver to care-team supervisor, taking on responsibility for coordinating multiple aides’ schedules, handling urgent family calls, and documenting care plans for a growing roster of elderly clients. The promotion dramatically increased the amount of information she had to juggle at once—phone calls, messaging apps, electronic records, and in-person conversations—while she continued to stay up late watching films and going to dance classes, leaving her mentally taxed. Over the ensuing year, she noticed that her mind constantly drifted to other tasks or outside distractions during important planning sessions and documentation work, causing mix-ups in schedules, missed follow-ups, and tension with both staff and families who depended on her accuracy. After a near-miss where a client’s medication visit was almost skipped due to her losing track of details during a hectic shift, her supervisor expressed concern and suggested she get an evaluation, prompting her to seek psychiatric help because she felt unable to keep her attention where it needed to be despite her strong motivation to do well.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I get distracted so easily at work that I lose track of what I’m doing, even when it’s important.”
